analysis.one_liner: Standardizes how banks advertise interest rates and requires plain-language disclosure of account fees.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 1991 with no cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never received a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required banks, thrifts, and credit unions to advertise savings yields using one standardized annual percentage yield, disclose all fees and account conditions in a plain-language schedule given to customers before they open an account, and stop calling accounts 'free' when minimum balances or transaction limits trigger fees. It also added civil liability for misleading advertising, required 30 days' notice before account terms got worse, and tightened disclosure for home equity loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers with checking and savings accounts, who would be able to compare rates and fees across banks on an apples-to-apples basis, learn fees before opening an account, and sue when advertising misrepresents an account.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every advertisement that mentions a yield to use a single standardized annual percentage yield and disclose minimum-balance requirements, fees that could reduce the yield, and early-withdrawal penalties [S2][S3]

Requires each institution to maintain and distribute a plain-language schedule of all fees, charges, minimum balances, and account terms, provided to potential customers before an account is opened [S2][S3]
Prohibits describing an account as free or no-cost if a minimum balance, transaction limit, or regular fee is required to avoid charges [S3]
Gives account holders the right to sue for actual damages plus $100–$1,000, or class damages up to $500,000, with attorney's fees for successful actions [S3]
Requires 30 days' mailed notice before any change that would reduce a yield or adversely affect an account holder [S3]
Amends the Truth in Lending Act to require home equity lenders to disclose the margin on variable-rate plans [S2][S3]

analysis.who_pays: Banks, savings institutions, and credit unions, which would bear the cost of standardized disclosures, revised advertising, and potential lawsuits; customers could also indirectly absorb compliance costs through fees.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for hundreds of depository institutions—new schedules, revised ads, and litigation exposure—could be passed to consumers through higher fees [S3]
The bill is disclosure-only: it does not cap any fee or rate, so banks could still charge high fees as long as they disclose them [S2][S3]

Liability is limited: a one-year statute of limitations, a bona fide error defense, class recovery capped at the lesser of $500,000 or 1% of net worth, and no liability if the bank notifies and corrects an error within 60 days [S3]
The Federal Reserve could exempt broadcast, electronic, and outdoor ads from key disclosures if it finds them unnecessarily burdensome, weakening the advertising rules [S2][S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For savers and checking customers the upside is real but modest: standardized yields and upfront fee schedules make comparison shopping possible and curb misleading 'free account' advertising. The bill does nothing to lower fees themselves, and its private right of action is hedged with caps and defenses, so its consumer value depends heavily on how the Federal Reserve writes the regulations. The main cost falls on financial institutions in compliance and litigation exposure.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking Committee in April 1991, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Sen. Christopher Dodd introduced the Truth in Savings and Investments Act on April 16, 1991 [S1][S5]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs on the day it was introduced [S5]
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never left committee and never received a floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Depository institutions avoided new advertising restrictions, mandatory fee schedules, and lawsuit exposure; consumers went without standardized yield and fee disclosure from this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Banks and credit unions, which avoided new disclosure rules

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out or scheduled any action

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors of either party, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never registered in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have restricted how banks advertise yields, banned 'free account' marketing when fees apply, required plain-language fee schedules, and exposed them to lawsuits. Banks benefit from competing on confusing ads and undisclosed fees, so their interest ran against the consumer protections.
Credit unions would face substantially similar disclosure rules written by their own regulator, with special accommodation for dividend-paying limits, so the burden was softened but not eliminated.

The bill required the SEC and Federal Reserve to review investment-company disclosure rules to make savings and investment products comparable, a potential precursor to stricter fund disclosure but imposing no immediate requirements.
